exercise.name: Inchworm

reference.title: Inchworm

exercise.mechanics: Compound (hip hinge to plank and back)

breathing.pattern: Breathe steadily while walking; exhale as you hold the plank; inhale as you stand.

prescription.frequency: As a warm-up or 2-3 times a week
prescription.progression: Walk further out (hands past the shoulders), add a push-up in the plank

cues.text: Hinge forward and put the hands on the floor in front of the feet, knees soft.
Walk the hands forward one at a time until you are in a high plank.
Hold a straight line from head to heels, hands under the shoulders.
Walk the hands back toward the feet, hips rising.

mistakes.fix: Brace the belly and squeeze the glutes.

mistakes.mistake: Locking the knees hard in the fold

kinematics.peak: Hands 28 cm ahead of the balls of the feet, knees ≈32°, hip flexion ≈133°
kinematics.norm: Hands to the floor with soft knees (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: Hands under the shoulders, 115 cm ahead of the balls of the feet; hips within ≈13° of the shoulder-ankle line, knees ≈0°
kinematics.norm: Hands under the shoulders, body straight (standard plank position)

kinematics.peak: 4 steps per hand of 22 cm, alternating (right first), hands lifting about 6 cm
Stay put; heels rise to a 60° foot pitch on the balls in the plank (ankle -6° to 35°)
kinematics.norm: Stay put; heels rise as the body lengthens into the plank (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: 1.2 s fold, 2.4 s walk out, 0.8 s plank, 2.4 s walk back, 1.2 s rise

sources.title: GymVisual #9044, Inchworm, video (movement reference; page not readable here)
Escamilla et al. 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379)
Ludewig, Hoff, Osowski, Meschke and Rundquist 2004, relative balance of serratus anterior and upper trapezius muscle activity during push-up exercises (Am J Sports Med 32(2):484-493)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Wrist discomfort: make fists or reduce the time on the hands.
Tight hamstrings: bend the knees more in the fold; do not force it.
modify: Bend the knees as much as needed to reach the floor.
progressions: Add a push-up at the plank.

muscleNotes.core: The abdominals hold the trunk rigid as the hands walk out into a long plank, the hardest point being the fully extended plank (clinical opinion; plank activity, Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Carries the body weight on the hands, more as they walk further out (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: Carries the body weight on the hands, more as they walk further out (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Holds the shoulder blades on the ribs in the plank (Ludewig 2004).
muscleNotes.serratus_l: Holds the shoulder blades on the ribs in the plank (Ludewig 2004).
muscleNotes.triceps_r: Keep the elbows straight under load (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.triceps_l: Keep the elbows straight under load (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_r: Keep the knees nearly straight (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Keep the knees nearly straight (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_max_r: Hold the hips in line in the plank and help stand back up (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.glute_max_l: Hold the hips in line in the plank and help stand back up (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: Lengthen in the forward fold with the knees nearly straight (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_l: Lengthen in the forward fold with the knees nearly straight (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.calves_r: Lengthen as the heels stay down in the fold (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.calves_l: Lengthen as the heels stay down in the fold (clinical opinion).
